title: How do you not lose confidence when you see the competition?
author: loontoon
selftext:
So I'm a month into building my game. 

I've just seen a similar game, that looks 1000 times better than mine does or probably ever will. 

I really feel like I'm wasting my time doing this now.

comments.author: CCB0x45
comments.body: I am hoping I am doing something unique so I don't have competition...

comments.author: CrimsonClockwerk
comments.body: It's not about the fact the other looks better but rather that you finish yours. Even if yours is "not as good" you still finished it. then you can move onto your next project with the experience you hold.

comments.author: Any_Ad_8450
comments.body: just remember, "everyone is stupid except you", and you'll be fine. -Ghandi

comments.author: net_ninja
comments.body:
I’m making my first game for myself.
As long as it’s fun to me and finished then it’s a win in my book.
Comparison is the thief of joy.

replies.author: lostforever2011
replies.body: Same here, the game i am making is for my own use so it does not bother me if others are doing better than me! i mean there will always be someone better than me so just shurg it off!

replies.author: Veilkam
replies.body: Same here, quitted my game Dev job to make my own game on my own term. Not expecting to make any money out of it, just want to be proud and prove myself that I can make it alone without loosing my head to stress and deadlines.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body: What are you living on?   I lost my job to AI and at 59 I have almost no savings and no pension, this is a hail mary.  And yes I know how crazy that sounds.

replies.author: Veilkam
replies.body:
Living out of my saving, had a more or less frugal lifestyle and good spending habit, my cost of living is way below average for my area so i was able to stack up a reasonable amount of cash.

I had to make sacrifices in the past and even bigger one now that i don't have any income, but it was worth it for the peace of mind.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body:
I've been in Bangkok for 18 years, I have cut back my spending by quitting drinking, rarely going out and eating healthy but cheap.  It still costs me $1000 a month for all my living costs.  I stacked up a bit but 2 years ago I expected a crypto bull run and put almost all my money into alts. My portfolio is down 70%.  I have maybe 10 months of living expenses until I have to start selling crypto. 

I was really hoping that crypto would recover by then but it's not looking good.  

I cannot find any work here so my only other option is try to make my own money.    
  
Every $1000 my game makes adds 1 month to the length of time I can wait for the crypto recovery.  Every 10K it makes give me the chance to try building another game or add features to this one of its that popular.  

Huge risk, but like I said its my last hail mary.

replies.author: Veilkam
replies.body: do not expect it to recover, its gone, sorry, alt coins are scams. Saying that from someone that hold crypto as well.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body: Not all of them are, some are real projects building things that one day everyone will use, like we all use http, smtp, etc....

comments.author: thebuddybud
comments.body:
Do it for fun.
If its fun, it can be good.

comments.author: ChanThe4th
comments.body:
I can give you a sports related story.

I grew up surrounded by people that were naturally talented at almost all contact sports. They were terrifying in the best way possible. Most of them had zero resistance going through school competition.

Then they went against equal opponents. One got knocked out, another choked out, one got put through a literal wall. It broke them down because they never experienced what being at the bottom felt.

So in one way you're worse and it's harder, in another way though it can only go up from here.

comments.author: samuele_v
comments.body:
As other people already said, in every creative endeavor and not just game-making with AI, you should build something you want, not somehing you compare with other people's stuff.

By all means, you should take a look at what is currently vibing (pun intended), but if your mindset is only about comparisons, it's a race you'll never win, as potentially there will always something better than what you created. Think of it as fuel to never stop improving.

(But yes. Eventually you'll need to stop improving and release what you created. :D)

comments.author: rdditiszionist
comments.body:
Imagine being able to use AI to make whatever the hell you want and you see someone doing what you are doing.

I think that is literally all your fault, OP.

it's like you can't be creative or something.

Make a game about a talking penny that exists in the 4th dimension, saving sentient pretzels from morbid tyrannical goldfish. And you as the player have to knit the talking penny a new sweater as his grandmother in the 9th dimension, so you can see and experience everything because he does.

like what are you even doing?

CARD GAME + DARK SOULS + 8 BIT + CYBER PUNK

zzzzzzzzzzzzzz

comments.author: LatentBlade
comments.body: My goal of building a deck builder is to spend less time playing slay the spire. And I play less.... I haven't even download STS 2.

replies.author: NormieInTheMaking
replies.body: Don't do that. You need to take inspirations from the best ones. If anything, I play more nowadays and my game's gotten better.

comments.author: Dependent_Yam_1028
comments.body:
Then you should be happy that others are making the game you want to make and support them. If someone was making the game im trying to make, id be thrilled. Would save me time and money lol. 

If its just about making a project and learning, like others are saying its about completing a project, not about breaking new ground in an overcrowded industry.

comments.author: HLCYSWAP
comments.body:
you have to think in longer timelines.

  
what that means is you need to understand that your first game isnt going to be your best game. narratively, it might be the best, but its not going to be the best quality. you arent going to have the most resources, the biggest marketing budget, etc. statistically you will not have your best release first 99.99% of the time. 

  
with that in mind, start orienting your mind towards understanding you will get better at this and your next game will take half the time, the next game half that, so on and so on. you will be releasing many games if this is your passion. 

  
so, think about your entire timeline, do not obsess about the first attempt. make it fun, get it out, learn. dont try to make perfection

comments.author: Joffie87
comments.body: so umm, are you comparing yourself to square or something? Lol just have fun and be passionate about what you're building.

comments.author: Enjoyooooor
comments.body: Me personally I see this as motivation to do better and refine what I am doing. What is better about the other game? You can see where you’re falling short now you find a way to improve and keep building.

comments.author: redtigerpro
comments.body: You are your own worst critic.  I bet there is someone looking at what you've built thinking "this is so much better than I could do"

comments.author: robogame_dev
comments.body:
Your game doesn’t have to be for everyone, it just has to be for you - and however many other people are like you. 

Sure you can see other people producing and publishing masterpieces. But their masterpiece doesn’t scratch the exact itches yours does, because they’re not you - it’s a different game, and yours doesn’t need to be the best to be valid, it just has to be different - to have your spin, your taste, your sensibilities woven throughout it.

Passion and personality beats polish every day of the week.

comments.author: vexmach1ne
comments.body:
Learn from it. Whoever made that better game didn't start yesterday. They gained skills by not giving up and by working hard. 

Just have fun and don't quit your day job.

comments.author: medigul
comments.body: If this is something you like then keep doing it. Don’t compare yourself to others along the way. You’ll see people who are better than you, but ofc, you’ll also see people who aren’t as good as you. Just make sure you're doing something you enjoy, that's it.

comments.author: test_test_1_2
comments.body: Really, do it for fun. It's funny because I am enjoying working on building a game as much as playing one. It's like, building a game nowadays is the actual game itself. It's a custom game and it feels great to see it evolve and grow.

comments.author: pizzae
comments.body: Your only 1 month in? Try being 12 months still prototyping, not even done yet. Rome wasn't built in a day, neither a month

replies.author: NormieInTheMaking
replies.body: How long did it take for Rome to be built? I need to know that before I can plan the development of my game.

comments.author: WearyVegetable2320
comments.body:
You should not be afraid of genuine competition. What is truly damaging is artificially created competition and fake crowds, which can become a nightmare for any legitimate small business or independent professional.

I hav seen this firsthand during tech hiring processes and, more recently, on freelancing platforms. No honest business can thrive for long if it's forced to compete against manipulated or fabricated competition.

On the other hand fair competition creates opportunities. If your product or service genuinely helps customers achieve their goals or fulfill their aspirations there will always be a way to earn and grow. It's many a times evident when you see how tiny and small tea stalls become more popular than million-dollar restaurants despite selling essentially the similar things.

comments.author: Putrid_Argument2440
comments.body: At least it means that you're representative. It's a big advantage. For me, with 25+ yoe in game development it's a problem - I have no issues with implementation and every decision I make with my inner voice is quite weird and not fun. So I have to decide basing on my experience and knowledge instead of imagination.

comments.author: Sea-Way4976
comments.body: I have basically none (maybe a horrible sign)

replies.author: Sea-Way4976
replies.body: If it feels like reality just set in, and your gut is telling you to give up, do it. You might feel like you wasted your time, but nothing is a waste of time as long as you can grow from it. Don’t throw out the things you’ve learned, do competitor analysis earlier next time, don’t avoid points of failure, take the things you’ve come to understand about memory, implementation, delegation, planning and be extremely deliberate with what your goal is so you can investigate every path you can take to get there. You might discover something in the process of growing that makes this path viable again. AI is amazing because you can trial and error faster than a studio could a couple years ago, take full advantage of that.

comments.author: FrozenFirebat
comments.body:
1) be part of the process, not the result.

2) you'll be surprised how much incremental improvements that seem like accidental improvements stack up (from somebody who is not creative)

3) Make the game you want to play, not the one that beats the market.

comments.author: AdStreet4350
comments.body: Well, because you're doing  the game for yourself first what competition ? And maybe inshallah It's going to sell, lmao

comments.author: captain_proton
comments.body:
Even if that is true you are still gaining experience and not sat around watching Netflix or something. It is a positive gain for you.

Maybe take a break from this project and focus on another. Ask yourself what is a unique twist you could add?

comments.author: davesoft
comments.body:
You have to make the game for yourself. It isn't 1992 anymore, we can't just get an exe that works and sell it.

If your determination to work on the project relies on it being popular, stop, roll over to a more interesting idea.

comments.author: donkeykong917
comments.body:
If everyone stopped because competition was fierce, you will never build or do anything lol

Get on with it.

comments.author: ididmr2
comments.body: The purpose has to be the process. If this is your medium for creative thinking and about, you're refining your skill.

comments.author: porky11
comments.body:
If your game is just like something that exists, but worse, it's not probably not worth putting more effort into it.
If there's something special about your game that other games don't have, the quality doesn't matter that much.

Also it's easy to generate things that look good at a first glance. When I saw all the games people created with fable in one prompt, and then looked at what I created with fable and other AI in weeks, I also felt a little discouraged.

But the games they created were usually created using web technology, and just short demos with the core functionality and nothing else. They don't know how to continue from there.
But whenever I create something, I end up with a bunch of tools which I can use in other games as well, even if I decide to drop some of my games I'm working on.

In my case, there's some stories I want to get out there. And I have some unique gameplay ideas. It's okay if the game doesn't look good. Graphics doesn't matter. Is it fun? Do you feel things when you play it? That's what matters more, I think.

comments.author: oVerde
comments.body: AFAIK great (game) designers only look sideways to steal as inspiration, they are too heads down into their crafting

comments.author: DigitalRealmsS
comments.body: If it’s your first game. And the scope is not too big, then just finish it and move on, you will learn a lot from doing this. But If it’s a big game I think I would pass on it and go for a smaller project with lower risk.

comments.author: Tangostorm
comments.body:
Put it in another perspective: how many restaurants are there? Why shoud I open another one if there are millions outsider? 

Because you want and love to do it.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body:
People open restaurants to make money.  I know lots of people who've opened bars and restaurants, none of them did it for any reason except to make money.  Some were hugely successful, some less so. 

I co-owned a late night club in Hong Kong that was a passion, but it cost me a huge amount of money to setup and I never made it the money back.

comments.author: LocoMod
comments.body: Try to get inspiration from it instead of losing confidence.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body: I'm just not that good at the visuals. I have loads of ideas for the gameplay, but actually making it look good is the problem.

comments.author: ResenhaDoBar
comments.body: The first 15 games you make will suck, go through them fast

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body: I'm 59.  This is my first and maybe last game.  If it makes nothing it will be my last game.  If it makes enough money to keep me alive, maybe I'll have enough money to try again.  But I'm not going to be able to keep coming up with complex game ideas.

comments.author: loontoon
comments.body:
Thanks everyone for the replies. 

I really appreciate them.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
I think it is a good sign because you are aware

When you do improve the game to the point where you can feel confident about its quality, then you would in a good position

comments.author: Ok-Investment4414
comments.body: fam tripple A games with blown out budgets are losing to indie ... its about the player and the loop

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body: Put yourself in the game, they can't compete with who you are.

comments.author: Roth_Skyfire
comments.body: Because there's more to a game than just how it looks. If you have something unique that people can't find in other games, there's nothing to really worry about.

comments.author: JiachengWu
comments.body: The competition is always yourself, so it you enjoy it, there is no competition
